'''''Casuarina equisetifolia''''', commonly known as '''coastal she-oak''', '''horsetail she-oak''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''incana'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Casuarina~equisetifolia |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=29 April 2023}}</ref> '''ironwood,'''<ref>{{Cite web |date=2009-12-24 |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' - Common Ironwood, Beach Sheoak, Horsetail Casuarina, Australian Pine, Australian Beefwood - Hawaiian Plants and Tropical Flowers |url=https://wildlifeofhawaii.com/flowers/774/casuarina-equisetifolia-common-ironwood/ |access-date=2023-10-27 |language=en-US}}</ref> '''beach sheoak''', '''beach casuarina''', '''whistling tree'''<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|page=82|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&pg=PA82}}</ref> or '''Australian pine'''<ref name="LP"/> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Casuarinaceae]] and is native to the Western Pacific, Australia, New Guinea, Southeast Asia and India. It is a small to medium-sized, [[Monoecy|monoecious]] tree with scaly or furrowed bark on older specimens, drooping branchlets, the leaves reduced to scales in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of 7 or 8, the fruit {{cvt|10–24|mm|1}} long containing winged seeds ([[Samara (fruit)|samara]]s) {{cvt|6–8|mm|sigfig=1}} long.

== Description ==
=== Habit ===
''Casuarina equisetifolia'' is an [[evergreen]] tree typically growing to a height of {{cvt|6–12|metres}}, sometimes to {{cvt|35|m}} tall. The bark of young specimens is smooth and greyish, older trees have scaly, greyish-brown to black bark.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa"/> 

===Foliage===
The foliage consists of slender, drooping branchlets up to {{cvt|30|cm}} long, the leaves reduced to scale-like teeth {{cvt|0.3–0.5|mm|sigfig=1}} long, arranged in whorls of 7 or 8 (occasionally 6) around the branchlets. The sections of branchlet between the leaf whorls (the "articles") are {{cvt|5–13|mm|sigfig=1}} long and {{cvt|0.5–1.0|mm|sigfig=1}} wide.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa"/>

=== Flowers ===
This species of ''Casuarina'' is [[monoecy|monoecious]] with male and female flowers produced on the same tree, unlike most other species of its same genus which are dioecious.<ref name=foa/> Its male and female [[inflorescence]]s are both shaped like [[catkin]]s.<ref name="LP"/> Its male flowers appear in simple spikes {{convert|0.7|–|4|cm|in|abbr=on}} long in whorls of 7 to 11.5 per cm (per 0.4 in), with [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] are {{cvt|0.6–0.8|mm|sigfig=1}} long, whereas its female flowers are {{cvt|3–13|mm|1}} long on short, sparsely hairy [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]].<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa"/>

=== Fruit ===
The [[fruit]] is an oval woody structure {{convert|10|–|24|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|9|–|13|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter when mature, superficially resembling a [[conifer cone]] made up of numerous [[Gynoecium|carpels]]. Each carpel contains a single small [[Samara (fruit)|winged seed]] {{convert|6|–|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name=foa>{{cite web |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528160946/https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Taxonomy and naming ==
The genus ''Casuarina'' was first formally described in 1759 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in ''[[Amoenitates Academicae]]'' and the first species he described was ''Casuarina equisetifolia''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Casuarina''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/457715|publisher=APNI|access-date=21 April 2023}}</ref><ref name="L.">{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Amoenitates academicae, seu, Dissertationes variae physicae, medicae, botanicae |date=1759 |page=143 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15496#page/146/mode/1up |access-date=29 April 2023}}</ref> The specific epithet ''equisetifolia'' means 'horsehair-leaved'.<ref name="Boland" />

In 1873, [[George Bentham]] described ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' var. ''equisetifolia'' and ''C. equisetifolia'' var. ''incana'' in ''[[Flora Australiensis]]'',<ref name="Benth.">{{cite book |last1=Bentham |first1=George |title=Flora Australiensis |volume=6 |date=1873 |publisher=Lovell Reeve & Co. |location=London |page=197 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/44539#page/203/mode/1up |access-date=29 April 2023}}</ref> and in 1982, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] changed the names to subspecies ''equisetifolia'' and ''incana'' respectively, in the ''[[Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens]]'':<ref name="JABG">{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Lawrence A.S. |title=Notes on Casuarinaceae II. |journal=Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens |date=1982 |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=79 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/61978679#page/91/mode/1up |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=29 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230429214411/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/61978679#page/91/mode/1up |url-status=live }}</ref>
* ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' <small>L.</small> subsp. ''equisetifolia'',<ref name="APC1">{{cite web|title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''equisetifolia''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55877|website=Australian Plant Census|access-date=29 April 2023|archive-date=29 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230429214409/https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55877|url-status=live}}</ref> a tree {{cvt|7–35|m}} high, the articles {{cvt|5–8|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|0.5–0.7|mm|sigfig=1}} wide with 8 to 10 teeth {{cvt|0.3–0.8|mm|sigfig=1}} long, the male spikes {{cvt|7–40|mm|1}} long, the cones {{cvt|12–24|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|9–11|mm|2}} wide on a peduncle {{cvt|3–10|mm|1}} long.<ref name="foa1">{{cite web|title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''equisetifolia''|url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia|publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra|access-date=29 April 2023|archive-date=28 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528160946/https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia|url-status=live}}</ref>
* ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''incana'' <small>(Benth.) L.A.S.Johnson.</small><ref name="APC2">{{cite web|title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''incana''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55881|website=Australian Plant Census|access-date=29 April 2023|archive-date=29 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230429214409/https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55881|url-status=live}}</ref> a tree {{cvt|6–12|m}} high, the articles {{cvt|7–13|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|0.7–1.0|mm|sigfig=1}} wide with 8 to 10 teeth about {{cvt|0.7|mm|sigfig=1}} long, the male spikes {{cvt|12–25|mm|1}} long, the cones {{cvt|10–20|mm|1}} long, {{cvt|10–13|mm|1}} wide and densely covered with white to rust-coloured hairs, on a peduncle {{cvt|3–13|mm|1}} long.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa2">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''incana'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528160946/https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20equisetifolia |url-status=live }}</ref> The epithet ''incana'' means 'white' or 'hoary'.<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |author=[[William T. Stearn]] |title=Botanical Latin. History, grammar, syntax, terminology and vocabulary |date=1992 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |edition=4th|page=431}}</ref>

There is some doubt as to whether Linnaeus' publication of ''C. equisetifolia'' is valid, since he based his description solely on [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius|Rumphius's]] description of ''Casuarina litorea'' in [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius#Herbarium Amboinense|Herbarium Amboinense]]<ref name="Rumphius">{{cite book |last1=Rumphius |first1=Georg E. |title=Herbarium Amboinense |volume=3 |date=1743 |location=Amsterdam |page=86 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/10353#page/142/mode/1up |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=29 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230429222122/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/10353#page/142/mode/1up |url-status=live }}</ref> and there are no [[Type (biology)|type]] specimens.<ref name="dcceew">{{cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=Flora of Australia |date=1989 |publisher=Australian Government Publishing Service |location=Canberra |page=201 |url=https://www.dcceew.gov.au/sites/default/files/env/pages/a08d125d-a6d0-47c4-85e9-9b7ac5d4931a/files/flora-australia-03-hamamelidales-casuarinales.pdf |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=16 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221016005614/https://www.dcceew.gov.au/sites/default/files/env/pages/a08d125d-a6d0-47c4-85e9-9b7ac5d4931a/files/flora-australia-03-hamamelidales-casuarinales.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

This species is sometimes given the common name "Australian pine" because it has features that seem superficially like those of a [[pine]], but it is not a [[conifer]].<ref name="LP">{{Cite web |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' |website=Landscape Plants |publisher=Oregon State University |url=https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/node/2144 |access-date=2023-10-28 |archive-date=2017-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504161107/https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/node/2144 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Casuarina equisetifolia'' subsp. ''equisetifolia'' grows near the sea, behind beaches and near [[Estuary|estuaries]], sometimes on rocky headlands in Australia, New Guinea, Southeast Asia and India.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="Boland" /> The species is native to [[India]] and [[Bangladesh]] in [[South Asia]]; [[Myanmar]], the [[Andaman Islands]], [[Nicobar Islands]], [[Vietnam]], [[Thailand]], [[Cambodia]], [[Peninsular Malaysia]], the [[Philippines]], [[Borneo]], [[Java]] and the [[Lesser Sunda Islands]], islands in the [[South China Sea Islands|South China Sea]], [[Sulawesi]] and [[Sumatra]] in Southeast Asia; [[Caroline Islands|the Carolines]], [[Fiji]], [[Mariana Islands|the Marianas]], the [[Marshall Islands]], [[New Caledonia]], [[Samoa]], [[Solomon Islands]], [[Tonga]], [[Tuvalu]] and [[Vanuatu]] in the Pacific Ocean; [[New Guinea]]; and [[New South Wales]], the [[Northern Territory]], and [[Queensland]] in Australia.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa1" />

Subspecies ''incana'' grows on rocky headlands near the coasts of eastern Queensland and New South Wales as far south as [[Laurieton]].<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa2" /><ref name="CIFR">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina equisetifolia'' |url=https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/AFTPDFS/Casuarina_equisetifolia.PDF |publisher=World Agroforestry (Centre for International Forestry Research) |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322130032/http://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/AFTPDFS/Casuarina_equisetifolia.PDF |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Casuarina equisetifolia'' has been introduced to many other continents and islands.<ref name="POWO" /> It is an [[invasive species]] in the United States, but biological control by insects, including by a ''[[Selitrichodes]]'' wasp and [[Carposinidae]] and [[Gelechiidae]] moths, has been effective.<ref>{{cite web|title=Biological control of Australian native ''Casuarina'' species in the 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605113952/http://www.csiro.au/science/ps334.html|archive-date=5 June 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Masterson|first=J|date=4 October ==Ecology==
''Casuarina equisetifolia'' is an [[actinorhizal plant]] able to [[Nitrogen fixation#Biological|fix]] atmospheric nitrogen<ref name="Wild Singapore">{{Cite web |url=http://www.wildsingapore.com/wildfacts/plants/coastal/casuarina/equisetifolia.htm |title=Rhu or Casuarina tree |last=Tan |first=Ria |date=October 2016 |website=Wild Singapore |access-date=25 October 2022 |archive-date=3 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220903081423/http://www.wildsingapore.com/wildfacts/plants/coastal/casuarina/equisetifolia.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> through a [[symbiosis|symbiotic relationship]] with strains of ''[[Frankia]]'', a [[Actinomycetales|actinomycete]] hosted in [[root nodule|nodule]]s on its roots.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=David R. |last2=Silvester |first2=Warwick B. |title=Biology of ''Frankia'' strains, actinomycete symbionts of actinorhizal plants |journal=Microbiological Reviews |date=June 1993 |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=293–319 |doi=10.1128/mr.57.2.293-319.1993 |pmid=8336669 |pmc=372911 }}</ref>{{rp|294}}

== Uses ==
Besides its ornamental uses, ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' has also been explored for its potential in remediation of textile dye wastewater. The leaves were found to be useful as absorbent material for the removal of textile dyes such as reactive orange 16,<ref name="Bharti">{{cite journal |last1=Bharti |first1=Vikash |last2=Shahi |first2=Amrita |last3=Geed |first3=Sachin |last4=Kureel |first4=M.K. |title=Biodegradation of reactive orange 16 dye in the packed bed bioreactor using seeds of ''Ashoka'' and ''Casuarina'' as packing media |journal=Indian Journal of Biotechnology |date=2017 |volume=16 |pages=216–221}}</ref> [[rhodamine B]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/23311843.2016.1140553 |title=The removal of rhodamine B dye from aqueous solution using ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' needles as absorbent |journal=Cogent Environmental Science |volume=2 |year=2016 |last1=Kooh |first1=Muhammad Raziq Rahimi |last2=Dahri |first2=Muhammad Khairud |last3=Lim |first3=Linda B.L. |issue=1 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2016SusEn...240553K }}</ref> [[methylene blue]], [[malachite green]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.aej.2015.07.005 |title=Application of ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' needle for the removal of methylene blue and malachite green dyes from aqueous solution |journal=Alexandria Engineering Journal |volume=54 |issue=4 |page=1253 |year=2015 |last1=Dahri |first1=Muhammad Khairud |last2=Kooh |first2=Muhammad Raziq Rahimi |last3=Lim |first3=Linda B.L. |doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[methyl violet 2B]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1155/2013/619819 |title=Removal of Methyl Violet 2B from Aqueous Solution Using ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' Needle |journal=ISRN Environmental Chemistry |volume=2013 |pages=1–8 |year=2013 |last1=Dahri |first1=Muhammad Khairud |last2=Kooh |first2=Muhammad Raziq Rahimi |last3=Lim |first3=Linda B. L. |doi-access=free }}</ref> Similarly, the dried cone was also reported to be able to remove rhodamine B<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1155/2016/9497378 |title=Remediation of Rhodamine B Dye from Aqueous Solution Using ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' Cone Powder as a Low-Cost Absorbent |journal=Advances in Physical Chemistry |volume=2016 |pages=1–7 |year=2016 |last1=Dahri |first1=Muhammad Khairud |last2=Kooh |first2=Muhammad Raziq Rahimi |last3=Lim |first3=Linda B. L. |doi-access=free }}</ref> and methyl violet 2B.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=January 2017|title=Water remediation using ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' cone as adsorbent for the removal of methyl violet 2B dye using batch experiment method|url=http://www.vinanie.com/jebr/articles/v6n1p34.html|journal=Journal of Environment & Biotechnology Research|volume=6|issue=1|pages=34–42|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170319160528/http://www.vinanie.com/jebr/articles/v6n1p34.html|archive-date=19 March 2017|via=ViNaNiE}}</ref> The bark was reported to be able to remove methylene blue.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Adsorption of methylene blue by ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' bark|url=http://en.cnki.com.cn/Article_en/CJFDTOTAL-ZKZX201006017.htm|journal=CNKI|access-date=2018-02-15|archive-date=2020-07-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200710084127/http://en.cnki.com.cn/Article_en/CJFDTOTAL-ZKZX201006017.htm}}</ref> Even the seed was found to be useful in dye removal of [[neutral red]] and malachite green.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2017 |title=Application of microwave-treated Casuarina equisetifolia seeds in adsorption of dyes |url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/jfas/article/view/168708 |journal=Journal of Fundamental and Applied Sciences |volume=9 |issue=7S |pages=458–471 |issn=1112-9867 |archive-date=2024-09-12 |access-date=2025-07-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240912135952/https://www.ajol.info/index.php/jfas/article/view/168708 |url-status=live }}</ref> The carbon derived from the cones of ''C.{{nbsp}}equisetifolia'' was found to be a good absorbent for [[landfill]] [[leachate]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1063/1.5002333 |title=Removal of organic fractions from landfill leachate by ''Casuarina equisetifolia'' activated carbon: Characteristics and absorption mechanisms |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1885 |page=020139 |year=2017 |last1=Alrozi |first1=Rasyidah |last2=Zubir |first2=Nor Aida |last3=Kamaruddin |first3=Mohamad Anuar |last4=Yusof |first4=Siti Noor Faizah Mohd |last5=Yusoff |first5=Mohd Suffian |issue=1 |bibcode=2017AIPC.1885b0139A }}</ref> while another laboratory also reported good absorbency for copper ions from aqueous solution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Muslim|first=A.|date=2017|title=AUSTRALIAN PINE CONES-BASED ACTIVATED CARBON FOR ADSORPTION OF COPPER IN AQUEOUS SOLUTION|url=http://jestec.taylors.edu.my/Vol%2012%20issue%202%20February%202017/12_2_1.pdf|journal=Journal of Engineering Science and Technology|volume=12|issue=2|pages=280–295}}</ref> Line planting of ''C.{{nbsp}}equisetifolia'' trees in coastal areas has been known to help control the force of the wind. In countries like India, it has been known as a suitable species for wasteland development.{{citation needed|date=August 2024}}

== Culture ==
In the [[Philippines]], the town of [[Agoo]] is named after the tree (known as ''agoho'' or ''aroo'' in the [[Ilocano language]]).<ref name="Sals">{{Cite book |title=The History of Agoo: 1578-2005 |last=Sals |first=Florent Joseph |date=2005 |publisher=Limbagan Printhouse |location=La Union |page=80 |language=en}}</ref>
